brief.summary_1line: Valmiki, moved by a hunter killing a bird, spontaneously utters the first metrical verse; Brahma then commands him to compose the epic of Rama.

image_candidates.scene_text: A hidden hunter shoots a male krauncha bird while it mates, as the grieving female cries beside the fallen body before the shocked sage Valmiki.
Valmiki stands by the clear Tamasa River with disciple Bharadwaja, raising his hand in sorrow as he utters the first poetic curse.
The four-faced god Brahma appears radiantly in Valmiki’s forest hermitage, blessing the sage and commanding him to compose the story of Rama.

deep.rich_summary: This chapter explains how the poetic form of the Ramayana is born. After hearing Narada recount Rama’s story, the sage Valmiki reflects on it deeply. While visiting the Tamasa River with his disciple Bharadwaja, he witnesses a hunter kill a male krauncha bird while it is with its mate. Moved by compassion and anger at the cruelty, Valmiki spontaneously utters a rhythmic curse against the hunter. He then realizes that his grief has formed a structured verse—the first shloka meter. Soon after, the creator god Brahma appears and commands Valmiki to compose the full story of Rama in this poetic form, promising divine insight so nothing he writes will be false. The moment matters because it mythically explains the origin of Sanskrit epic poetry and establishes the Ramayana as a divinely sanctioned narrative.

highlight_spans.why: The opening marker situates the reader in the Bala Kanda, the beginning of the epic where its poetic origin story unfolds.
The killing of the male krauncha bird and the lament of its mate create the emotional shock that inspires Valmiki’s first poetic verse.
Valmiki’s curse to the hunter forms the first metrical shloka, traditionally considered the birth of Sanskrit epic poetry.
Brahma’s appearance reveals the divine mandate: Valmiki must compose the story of Rama with supernatural knowledge.
Brahma’s declaration that Rama’s story will endure as long as mountains and rivers exist frames the Ramayana as an eternal sacred epic.

top_scenes.scene_text: Valmiki stands by the forest river as a hunter’s arrow strikes the male krauncha bird mid-flight while its mate cries in grief beside the fallen body.
The four-faced god Brahma appears in radiant light before the astonished sage Valmiki inside the hermitage, commanding him to compose the story of Rama.
Valmiki, overcome with compassion, raises his hand and pronounces the first metrical verse while the mourning bird cries above the forest clearing.
